passage:
Monday. Madhav, eleven, told his little brother Shankar he would stop walking him to school if Shankar kept taking his cricket bat without asking.
Wednesday. At breakfast they fought again, this time over a torn comic. "I hate sharing a room with you!" Madhav shouted, and ate his poha facing the wall. After school, at the bus stop, a Class 7 boy grabbed Shankar's water bottle and held it high, laughing. Madhav dropped his bag. "Give it back. Now." His voice shook, but he stepped right up. The boy tossed the bottle down and left.
Saturday. Shankar took the bat again. Madhav opened his mouth, closed it, and said, "Fine. Bring it back with no mud."

qa.q: What did the Class 7 boy grab from Shankar?
qa.a: He grabbed Shankar's water bottle and held it high, laughing.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel toward Shankar that Wednesday morning, and what changed at the bus stop?
qa.a: In the morning he was angry enough to shout "I hate sharing a room with you!", but when Shankar was picked on, protectiveness pushed the anger aside.

qa.q: When Madhav stepped up at the bus stop, what choice was he making?
qa.a: He chose to face an older boy for his brother despite their fight, staying firm with words even though his voice shook.

qa.q: How might Shankar see his big brother by Saturday?
qa.a: Shankar may feel his brother is on his side even when they fight, which might be why he dares to take the bat again.

grounding: Across a week, a child who quarrelled with his brother that morning still stands up to a bully for him, and the grudge softens afterwards.

passage: Imran, come, sit. You fought with your sister again? Your Usha aunty was nine once, you know, and my little sister Leela and I quarrelled every single day. One morning she cut my red ribbon to make a doll's scarf. I screamed and told her she was no sister of mine. That same evening, at the village pump, two older boys splashed her and pulled her plait until she cried. I didn't think at all. I marched over with my bucket and said, "Touch her again and I'll tell the whole school, and your mothers." My knees were knocking. They went. Leela held my hand all the way home, ribbon forgotten. That is how it is, beta. You can be angry with your own and still stand in front of them.

qa.q: What did Leela cut to make a doll's scarf?
qa.a: Leela cut Usha's red ribbon to make a doll's scarf.

qa.q: How did young Usha feel as she marched over to the boys, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was scared, since her knees were knocking, but her anger at the boys for hurting Leela was stronger than the morning's grudge.

qa.q: What choice in the story might Imran carry into quarrels at home?
qa.a: Imran might decide that a fight at home is no reason to leave a sister alone when someone outside picks on her.

qa.q: What might Leela have felt, holding Usha's hand all the way home?
qa.a: Leela probably felt safe and forgiven, knowing her sister would protect her even after the ribbon fight.

grounding: An elder recalls defending her little sister from bullies on the same day they had quarrelled, showing family loyalty overriding a grudge.

passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the bus shelter, and the school van was already twenty minutes late. Omkar, ten, stood as far as he could from his brother Tushar. That morning Tushar had spilled milk on Omkar's finished map homework, and Omkar had not spoken to him since. Then a Class 6 boy started kicking puddle water at Tushar's shoes. "Wet baby," he sneered. Tushar's lip wobbled. Omkar crossed the shelter in three steps. "Stop it. He's my brother." The older boy was a head taller. Omkar didn't move, even as water soaked his socks. When the van finally splashed up, Omkar pushed Tushar in first and sat beside him, still not talking, but shoulder to shoulder.

qa.q: What had Tushar spilled that morning?
qa.a: Tushar had spilled milk on Omkar's finished map homework.

qa.q: Why did Omkar sit shoulder to shoulder with Tushar yet still not talk?
qa.a: He still felt hurt about the ruined homework, but he wanted his brother close and safe after the bully 😔

qa.q: What could Omkar do once they're home about the morning's quarrel?
qa.a: He could tell Tushar he is still upset about the map and ask him to help redraw it, so the grudge gets settled instead of lingering.

qa.q: What was it like for Tushar to see Omkar step in despite the quarrel?
qa.a: Tushar probably felt relieved and a little surprised, learning that his brother protects him even while angry with him.

grounding: A child still cross with his brother from the morning defends him from an older bully in the rain, loyalty outweighing the grudge.

passage: That morning Deepika, ten, and her brother Varun had fought over the TV remote so loudly that Mummy took it away. "You're the worst brother ever," Deepika said, and didn't talk to him at breakfast. In the evening, at the park in their Nagpur colony, Varun was flying his new kite. A bigger boy from the next building, maybe twelve, grabbed the string and yanked it. The kite tore on a branch. "Baby kite for a baby," the boy said. Varun's chin shook. Deepika was across the park on the swings. She jumped off and ran over, her heart hammering. "Give that string back. He's my brother." The boy was taller, but she didn't move. He dropped the string and walked off. Deepika picked up the torn kite, smoothed it and handed it to Varun. She still didn't say sorry about the remote.

qa.q: What did the bigger boy do to Varun's kite?
qa.a: He grabbed the string and yanked it, and the kite tore on a branch.

qa.q: How can you tell Deepika was scared when she stood up to the boy?
qa.a: Her heart was hammering and the boy was taller, but she still did not move.

qa.q: What choice did Deepika make, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She put aside the morning's fight and ran to defend Varun, showing that family loyalty mattered more to her than the grudge.

qa.q: How might Varun see his sister after the park?
qa.a: Varun may feel protected and surprised, knowing his sister stood up for him on the same day she called him the worst brother.

grounding: A girl who fought with her brother that morning still rushes to defend him from a bigger boy, as family loyalty overrides the grudge.

passage:
"You broke my pencil box, Chinmay! I'm never lending you anything again." Charu slammed her door that morning.

In the afternoon their cousin Neeraj, fourteen, came to stay.
"What's this?" Neeraj held up Chinmay's drawing. "A dog? Looks like a potato."
Chinmay, eight, reached for it. "Give it back."
"Potato-dog! Potato-dog!" Neeraj held it over his head.
Charu came out of her room. "Neeraj bhaiya, give it back."
"Why? You're not even talking to him."
"He's still my brother." Her voice wobbled, but she held out her hand. "Give it. Now."
Neeraj rolled his eyes and handed it over. "Fine. So touchy."
Charu gave the drawing to Chinmay. "It's a good dog."
"You're not angry any more?"
"I'm still angry about the pencil box," Charu said. "That's different."

qa.q: What did Neeraj say Chinmay's drawing looked like?
qa.a: He said it looked like a potato.

qa.q: What does Charu's wobbling voice suggest when she faces Neeraj?
qa.a: It suggests she was nervous standing up to an older cousin but did it anyway to protect her brother.

qa.q: What does Charu's last line teach about family loyalty?
qa.a: It shows she can stay angry about the pencil box and still defend Chinmay, because loyalty to him matters more than the grudge.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel about his sister after this?
qa.a: Chinmay might feel relieved and loved, surprised that the sister who slammed her door in the morning stood up for him.

grounding: A girl defends her little brother from an older cousin's teasing on the same day she quarrelled with him, showing loyalty over a grudge.

passage: That morning Chandrika, ten, and her little brother Chintu had fought over the last jalebi, and she'd told him she'd never talk to him again. In the afternoon, walking back from the village school past the pond, she saw a bigger boy from the next lane holding Chintu's slate high above his head. Chintu was jumping and crying. Chandrika didn't think. She marched straight over, stood between them and said, "Give it back. Now." Her heart hammered; the boy was a head taller. Her friend Yusuf came and stood beside her. The boy shrugged and dropped the slate. Chandrika picked it up, wiped it on her frock, and took Chintu's hand. At home they told Amma at once. Amma listened, then walked with them to the boy's house to speak to his parents before dinner.

qa.q: What was the bigger boy holding above his head?
qa.a: He was holding Chintu's slate high above his head.

qa.q: What was Chandrika feeling as she stood between them?
qa.a: Chandrika felt protective and scared at once, her heart hammering because the boy was a head taller.

qa.q: What did Amma do that helped?
qa.a: Amma listened and went with them to speak to the boy's parents before dinner, so the bullying was dealt with the same day.

qa.q: How might Chintu have felt when Chandrika stepped in, after their morning fight?
qa.a: Chintu likely felt relieved and protected, perhaps surprised his sister came to help after saying she'd never talk to him again.

grounding: A child who quarrelled with her brother that morning fiercely defends him from a bully, showing family loyalty overriding a grudge.

passage: At breakfast in their Berlin flat, Selin, eleven, had screamed at her younger brother Tariq for using her hairbrush on the dog. "I hate you!" she'd said. At the school playground that afternoon, she saw three older boys pushing Tariq against the fence, calling him "baby." Something hot rose in her chest. She dropped her bag and ran over. "Leave him alone!" One of the boys laughed. Selin's legs were shaking, but she stepped closer. "I'll get Frau Weber right now." They backed off. Tariq's lip was trembling. Selin put an arm round him, marched him straight to Frau Weber and told her everything. The teacher listened, took the boys' names, and phoned their mother before home time. On the walk home Tariq whispered, "You said you hated me." Selin shrugged. "I do. Only I'm allowed to."

qa.q: What were the older boys calling Tariq?
qa.a: They were calling him "baby."

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when something hot rose in her chest?
qa.a: Selin felt fiercely protective and angry, strong enough to override her morning resentment.

qa.q: Why was taking Tariq to Frau Weber straight away a good choice?
qa.a: It brought in an adult who could stop the bullying the same day and contact their mother.

qa.q: How might Tariq have felt when Selin put her arm around him?
qa.a: Tariq probably felt safe and relieved, and perhaps touched that his sister defended him despite the morning fight.

grounding: A child who quarrelled with her brother that morning fiercely defends him from bullies, showing family loyalty overriding a grudge.

passage: At the Pune school's bus stop, Sarika, nine, stood apart from her twin brother Mintu. They'd fought that morning over who got the window seat, and she wasn't speaking to him. Then a group of older kids started snatching Mintu's cap and throwing it between them. Mintu's face crumpled. Sarika's grudge vanished. She pushed through, grabbed the cap in mid-air, and said loudly, "Stop it. He's my brother." Her classmate Francis stood next to her. The older kids muttered and moved away. Sarika handed Mintu the cap. Then she went straight to the bus conductor aunty and told her what had happened. The aunty wrote down the older kids' names and said she'd tell the class teacher that afternoon. On the bus, Sarika gave Mintu the window seat.

qa.q: What were the older kids throwing between them?
qa.a: They were throwing Mintu's cap between them.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when Mintu's face crumpled?
qa.a: Sarika felt protective and angry, her grudge vanishing as loyalty took over.

qa.q: What did Sarika do after the cap that was sensible?
qa.a: She reported it to the bus conductor aunty, who took names and planned to tell the teacher that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Mintu feel when Sarika gave him the window seat?
qa.a: Mintu likely felt grateful and surprised, the morning's fight replaced by his sister's care.

grounding: A child who quarrelled with her twin that morning defends him from bullies, showing family loyalty overriding a small grudge.

passage:
Kashish, you fight with your sister every day? So did I, beta. I'm Anjali, your Nani, and my younger sister and I once didn't speak for three whole days over a hair ribbon.
On the third morning, she called me a thief in front of our whole family. I was so angry I didn't eat breakfast.
That afternoon, on the way back from school, two older boys started throwing mud at her new frock. She stood there crying.
I forgot all about the ribbon. I ran and stood in front of her with my school bag held up like a shield. "Leave my sister alone!" I shouted. They laughed, but they left.
She held my hand all the way home. Neither of us mentioned the ribbon again.

qa.q: What did Anjali and her sister fight over?
qa.a: They fought over a hair ribbon.

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling when she saw the boys throwing mud?
qa.a: She felt protective and fierce, forgetting her anger from the morning because her sister needed her.

qa.q: What choice did young Anjali make, and what else could she have done?
qa.a: She ran to stand in front of her sister; she could also have called a nearby adult or told their parents that evening so the boys were stopped.

qa.q: How did Anjali's sister feel on the walk home?
qa.a: She likely felt safe and grateful, holding Anjali's hand all the way home.

grounding: Shows, as an elder's memory, a child defending her younger sister from bullies on the same day they had quarrelled.

passage:
It was pouring, and the school bus was forty minutes late. Bidisha stood under the shed, not speaking to her little sister Nirmala. That morning Nirmala had spilled ink on Bidisha's homework, and Bidisha had shouted at her.
Two older girls from another school were waiting too. One grabbed Nirmala's umbrella. "Share, na." They laughed and held it out of reach.
Nirmala's lip trembled. She looked at Bidisha.
Bidisha was still angry. But she stepped forward. "Give it back. She's my sister." Her voice cracked, but she didn't move.
They dropped it. The bus came. Bidisha sat next to Nirmala and, without a word, held the umbrella over both of them to the door.

qa.q: How late was the school bus?
qa.a: The bus was forty minutes late.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have been feeling when her voice cracked?
qa.a: She was nervous and still a little angry, but her loyalty to Nirmala was stronger than her grudge.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do if the older girls bother them again?
qa.a: She could tell the bus conductor or a teacher, so an adult can stop the older girls.

qa.q: What is it like for Nirmala when Bidisha steps forward?
qa.a: Nirmala feels relieved and protected, even though her sister had been angry with her that morning.

grounding: Shows a child defending her younger sister from bigger girls on the same morning they quarrelled, in the rain.

passage: Monsoon mornings meant one umbrella for two, and that morning Nitin and Damini fought over it all the way to the gate. "You always hold it on your side!" "Because I'm taller!" She stomped ahead, soaked, and ignored him all day. At the bus stop after school, two older boys circled her. "Wet cat," one sneered, flicking water at her bag. Damini's chin wobbled. Nitin didn't think. He pushed between them and opened the umbrella over her. "Leave my sister alone." His voice cracked but he stood there. The boys shrugged and wandered off. The bus conductor said, "Next time, tell a teacher too, beta." At home, Mama heard the story and wrote to the class teacher that evening. Damini shared the umbrella on the walk home.

qa.q: What did Nitin and Damini fight over that morning?
qa.a: They fought over the umbrella.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: He was scared of the older boys but felt fiercely protective of Damini, so his loyalty beat both his fear and the morning's anger.

qa.q: How could Nitin handle bullying like this next time?
qa.a: Along with standing by his sister, he could tell a teacher, as the conductor suggested, so an adult deals with the older boys.

qa.q: How might Damini see her brother after the bus stop?
qa.a: She might feel protected and grateful, seeing that he stood up for her even though they had fought all day.

grounding: Illustrates a child defending his sister from bullies even after quarrelling with her that morning.

passage: "You broke my kite reel!" Nikita shouted before breakfast on Sankranti morning. "It was already broken!" Sachin shouted back. By noon they were flying separate kites from opposite ends of the terrace. Then a bigger boy from the next building leaned over the wall and yanked Nikita's string. "This is mine now." "Give it back!" Nikita's eyes filled. Sachin dropped his own kite. "That's my sister's. Give it back." "Or what?" "Or I'm getting Uncle from downstairs right now." The boy glanced toward the stairs. He threw the kite onto the terrace. Sachin picked it up and handed it to her. "Still angry about the reel?" she sniffed. "Yes," he said. "Doesn't matter." Uncle from downstairs came up anyway and spoke to the boy's parents.

qa.q: What did Nikita accuse Sachin of before breakfast?
qa.a: Breaking her kite reel.

qa.q: How can you tell Sachin was still upset with Nikita even as he helped her?
qa.a: When she asks if he's still angry about the reel, he says "Yes"; he still feels resentful but his protective loyalty matters more.

qa.q: Which part of Sachin's response worked, and why?
qa.a: Saying he would fetch Uncle from downstairs worked, because the bigger boy knew an adult would step in.

qa.q: What would change if Sachin had kept flying his own kite?
qa.a: Nikita would have faced the bigger boy alone, and she might have learned that their fight counted for more than being family.

grounding: Shows a child defending his sister from a bully despite their quarrel that morning.

passage: In the summer holidays, Darshan and I share one bicycle, and that morning he took it without asking. I shouted at him so loudly that Mummy came out. We weren't speaking at lunch. In the evening I went to the ground and saw a bigger boy holding my brother's shoe up high. "Torn shoes, torn shoes," he was singing. Darshan was trying not to cry. I forgot about the bicycle. I walked straight up, even though the boy was a head taller. "Give it back to him." He laughed, but he dropped it. I'm Gautam, Darshan's big brother, and my knees were shaking. When we got home I told Mummy, and she went to the boy's house that same evening. Darshan still takes the bicycle sometimes. I let him.

qa.q: What was the bigger boy singing?
qa.a: "Torn shoes, torn shoes."

qa.q: How was Gautam feeling as he walked up to the bigger boy?
qa.a: Gautam was afraid, since his knees were shaking, but he felt fiercely protective and forgot his anger about the bicycle.

qa.q: What did Gautam do after they got home, and why did it help?
qa.a: He told Mummy, and she went to the boy's house that same evening, so an adult could stop the teasing from happening again.

qa.q: What might Darshan think about his brother after that evening?
qa.a: Darshan might feel safe and grateful, realising that even after a big fight his brother was on his side.

grounding: Illustrates a child fiercely defending his younger brother from a bully after quarrelling with him the same day.

passage:
Teacher's note, Eid week, playground duty
Rehana (Class 6) and her younger sister Rukhsar (Class 3) arrived not speaking, after a fight over a hair clip that morning. At lunch, a bigger boy from Class 7 grabbed Rukhsar's tiffin and held it over her head. Rehana came across the playground at a run, stood between them and said, "Give it back. Now." Her voice was shaking, but she did not move. The boy handed it back. Rehana then walked off without a word to her sister, still sulking. I spoke to the Class 7 boy and informed his class teacher and our counsellor the same afternoon. I also told Rehana privately that she was brave, and that next time she can call a teacher too.
Farah, playground duty

qa.q: What did the two sisters fight over that morning?
qa.a: A hair clip.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel as she stood between the boy and Rukhsar?
qa.a: She felt scared, her voice shaking, but fiercely protective of her sister despite still being angry about the morning.

qa.q: What did Farah do next, and why was it right?
qa.a: Farah spoke to the Class 7 boy and told his class teacher and the counsellor the same afternoon, and reminded Rehana she can call a teacher too, so she need not face bullies alone.

qa.q: How might Rukhsar feel after Rehana rescued her tiffin?
qa.a: Rukhsar might feel grateful and safe, and a little confused, since her sister protected her but still walked off sulking.

grounding: A child defends her younger sister from a bully even though they quarrelled that morning.
